headline: Built to keep facts, the web spreads fakes too
dek: In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee proposed a way for one lab to stop losing what it knew.

slides.label: The bright idea
slides.title: Stop losing what people know
slides.text: At CERN, the physics lab near Geneva, people often stayed about two years, and what they knew left with them. In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee proposed linked documents anyone could reach.
slides.alt: Aerial view of CERN's main site near Geneva: low lab buildings, parking lots and roads set among farm fields and woods
slides.credit: CERN's main site near Geneva from the air, 2012. Brücke-Osteuropa. CC0.

slides.label: It worked
slides.title: One site, then 1.49 billion
slides.text: The first web server ran at CERN by Christmas 1990. In April 1993 CERN put the software in the public domain. By the end of 1994 there were 10,000 servers. Netcraft now counts about 1.49 billion sites.
slides.alt: A black NeXT computer and monitor in a museum case, with a handwritten label on the computer reading "This machine is a server. DO NOT POWER IT DOWN!!"
slides.credit: The NeXT computer that ran the first web server, shown at CERN, 2005. Coolcaesar. CC BY-SA 3.0.

slides.label: Wait, what?
slides.title: No one to ask
slides.text: The design had no gatekeeper. In his words, it was built on there being "no central authority" you had to ask for permission. Anyone could publish a page or link to any other. That was the point.

slides.label: The backfire
slides.title: Open to everyone, scams too
slides.statLabel: phishing attacks counted by the Anti-Phishing Working Group in 2025
slides.text: With no gate, anyone can put up a page that looks like your bank. In 2017 Berners-Lee wrote that it was too easy for misinformation to spread on the web, and that online political ads needed transparency.

slides.label: Could anyone have seen it coming?
slides.title: Abuse, yes. This scale, no.
slides.text: Abuse of open networks was not new: the first mass ad email went out in 1978, and a worm crippled thousands of computers in 1988. The scale was not foreseeable: the 1989 proposal was for one lab, and in late 1993 there were just over 500 web servers.

slides.label: The cleanup
slides.title: The inventor's repair kit
slides.text: In 2018 Berners-Lee started Inrupt to build Solid, which keeps your data in a personal store you control. In 2019 his Web Foundation launched the Contract for the Web: nine principles for governments, companies and citizens. In 2024 the foundation announced it was closing.

slides.label: The ledger
slides.title: Worth it?
gains: About 1.49 billion sites counted by Netcraft, July 2026
Free to use and build on: CERN released the code to the public domain in 1993
About 6 billion people online in 2025, three in four people on Earth (ITU)
costs: $20.9 billion in internet crime losses reported to the FBI in 2025, by email, phone and apps as well as the web
Misinformation that spreads because it gets clicks, by his own account
slides.text: The web put most of the world's knowledge a click away. It also opened a door that nobody guards.

slides.label: Credit for trying
slides.title: We owe him one
slides.text: Berners-Lee took on a real problem, knowledge walking out the door, and his answer was made free, with no patent and no royalties. When the costs showed up, he named them in public, and he is still building fixes.

slides.label: How the pattern works
slides.title: The gate came down
slides.text: Before the web, publishers, editors and broadcasters decided what reached the public. The web removed that gate, on purpose. The job of checking what is true, and who is selling what, didn't disappear. It moved to every reader.

slides.label: How you do this
slides.title: Your open doors move work too
slides.text: You launch an open API with no sign-up so developers can start in a minute. Usage takes off. So do scrapers and spam bots, and your support team spends its week telling real users from abuse. The checking didn't go away. It moved.
also: An open comment section that someone now has to moderate
A sign-up form with no check that fills with spam

slides.label: Lessons
slides.title: What we take from it
items: Removing a gatekeeper also removes the work the gate was doing.
A design that fits a lab of colleagues can behave very differently when the whole world joins.
An open design hands every reader the job of deciding what to trust.
